title: Resource curse

definition.text: The idea that countries rich in natural resources such as oil and minerals often see slower economic growth, weaker democracy or worse development than countries with fewer resources.

facts.text: Richard Auty first used the term 'resource curse' in 1993 for mineral-rich countries that grew more slowly than countries without plentiful resources.
The idea is older: in 1711 The Spectator observed that the most plentiful countries often had the poorest living.
A 1995 study by Jeffrey Sachs and Andrew Warner found a strong link between resource abundance and poor economic growth.
The IMF counts 51 countries as resource-rich, meaning at least 20% of exports or 20% of government revenue comes from nonrenewable resources; 29 of them are low or lower-middle income.
Oil and mineral prices swing widely, so governments that depend on them face volatile revenues that disrupt planning and debt payments.
Extraction tends to form an enclave with few links to the rest of the economy, and its high profits draw the best workers and investment away from other industries.
Countries whose economies are dominated by extraction tend to be less democratic and more corrupt; petroleum is the resource most consistently tied to weaker institutions.
Most experts think the curse is not universal or inevitable, but strikes certain kinds of countries under certain conditions.

contested_note: There is no academic consensus on whether resource abundance harms development; studies with empirical support reach contradictory findings.

definition.text: The large, sudden swings in government income that come from depending on natural resources whose prices fluctuate widely.

facts.text: Crude oil rose from $10 a barrel to $145 a barrel between 1998 and 2008, then fell by more than half to $60 in a few months.
In 2005, 99.3% of Angola's exports came from oil and diamonds alone.
Abrupt revenue changes often lead to broken contracts or cuts to social programmes, eroding the rule of law and public support.

definition.text: The tendency of a petrostate to start international conflicts or to be the target of them.

facts.text: Jeff Colgan's 2013 book popularised the term, finding that petrostates (10% or more of GDP from petroleum) are 250 percent more likely to start international conflicts than a typical country.
It remained unclear whether the same pattern holds for resources other than oil.

definition.text: The argument that heavy reliance on foreign aid can harm a country's development in the long run in the same way as the resource curse.

facts.text: Like resource revenue, aid is unearned income that can weaken politicians' accountability to citizens and reduce pressure to reform.
When aid is a major source of government revenue, it can reduce the incentive to build a tax system and respond to taxpayers.

title: Resource depletion

definition.text: The using up of a natural resource faster than it can be replaced.

facts.text: A resource's value depends on how much of it exists in nature and how costly it is to extract; under supply and demand, scarcer resources become more valuable.
Types of depletion include wetland and ecosystem degradation, soil erosion, aquifer depletion and overfishing.
Extraction of both renewable and non-renewable resources rose sharply with the Industrial Revolution, as new technology and economic growth raised demand.
Although rooted in colonialism and industrialisation, depletion has been a major concern only since the 1970s.
Wealthy nations have been described as outsourcing resource depletion to poorer nations, which suffer the greatest ecosystem losses.
The tragedy of the commons is used to explain many forms of resource depletion.

distinct_from: Fixed stock versus opportunity cost paradigm

title: Depletion accounting

definition.text: A form of green accounting that adjusts national accounts for the using up of natural resources, so that nature's value counts alongside the market economy.

facts.text: It uses country data to estimate the adjustments needed for the use and depletion of a nation's natural capital.
Environmentalists use it to track resource use over time and hold governments to account; economists use it to see how reliant countries or firms are on non-renewable resources.
It is hard to implement because nature is less quantifiable than cars or bread: choosing a unit of account and drawing ecosystem boundaries are major problems.

distinct_from: Fixed stock versus opportunity cost paradigm

title: Peak minerals

definition.text: A model of how the costs and impacts of mining change as ore quality declines before and after a region's mineral production peaks.

facts.text: It compares the cheap, easily reached ores mined before peak production with the costlier ores that follow.
Falling average ore grades are the key sign that production is getting more expensive, with deeper mines, more energy use and more waste rock.
Unlike coal, oil or phosphorus, most non-energy minerals and metals are unlikely to run out.

distinct_from: Fixed stock versus opportunity cost paradigm

title: Fixed stock versus opportunity cost paradigm

definition.text: A debate over whether to treat a mineral resource as a fixed physical stock, or to measure its usable amount through its price and opportunity cost.

facts.text: How best to describe resource depletion analytically is still debated.
Tilton and Lagos (2007) argued the opportunity cost view is better because price and opportunity cost represent the usable quantity.
Because total stocks and future markets are unknown, most economists do not see physical scarcity as a good guide to a resource's availability.

contested_note: Sources describe the question of how to model depletion analytically as an ongoing debate.

title: Groundwater as a non-renewable resource
article: Resource depletion#Groundwater as a non-renewable resource

definition.text: The view that much groundwater is effectively non-renewable because it refills far too slowly to be replaced within human lifetimes.

facts.text: Less than six percent of the world's water is replenished on a human timescale of 50 years.
Of the groundwater used for farming, 16–33% is non-renewable.
Overusing groundwater can lower water levels and dry up streams, harming surface ecosystems.

distinct_from: Fixed stock versus opportunity cost paradigm
